bib.title: TinyStories: How Small Can Language Models Be and Still Speak Coherent English?

read.skipped: Per-model completion tables (Figs 6-12) were read only in part; their body text is word-per-line noise. Figure 4 score table is an image and absent from the text.

question: How small can a language model be, in parameters and architecture, and still produce fluent, coherent English stories when trained on a dataset restricted to a 3-4 year-old's vocabulary?
hypothesis: Small models fail at coherence because of the breadth and diversity of web corpora, not because language is intrinsically complex; a refined synthetic dataset should let tiny models speak coherently.
contributions: TinyStories can train and evaluate SLMs below 10M parameters (embedding dim 256) or with one transformer block that still produce fluent, consistent stories
GPT-4-graded evaluation paradigm (GPT-Eval) giving grammar, creativity, consistency, plot scores
Training takes under a day on one GPU and shows scaling laws and width/depth trade-offs
Small models appear more interpretable (attention heads and MLP neurons)

method.summary: GPT-3.5/GPT-4 generate short stories from prompts seeded with random words (one verb, noun, adjective) and random story features; GPT-Neo-architecture models of about 1M to 80M parameters are trained on them and graded by GPT-4 on story completions. Diversity/memorisation is checked with Rouge overlap against the training set.
method.task: next-token pretraining on synthetic children's stories; story completion and instruction following

datasets.name: TinyStories
datasets.source: Generated by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 from a ~1500-word vocabulary (nouns, verbs, adjectives); 3 random words plus a random feature subset per story; released on Huggingface as TinyStories
datasets.preprocessing: Stories 2-3 paragraphs (sample prompt asks 3-5 paragraphs); tokenizer keeps top 10K GPT-Neo tokens

datasets.name: TinyStories-Instruct
datasets.source: Each story prefixed with a random subset of: word list, a sentence from the story (any but first), feature list, 1-2 line GPT-3.5 summary

datasets.name: TinyStories-Instruct-OOD
datasets.source: Instruct variant with no entry combining both Summary and Words instructions

datasets.name: GPT-Eval prompts
datasets.size: around 50 manually written story beginnings; 50 instruction sets for Instruct eval

models.name: TinyStories models (1M/3M/9M/28M/33M/1Layer/2Layer, up to ~80M)
models.params: roughly 1M to 35M in Section 4; largest about 80M
models.tokenizer: GPT-Neo tokenizer restricted to top 10K most common tokens
models.layers: 1 to 8 in Section 4 (2,4,8,12 in scaling study)
models.heads: 2,4,8 in head study; 16 in the interpretability 1-layer model

other.examples: 1M 8 layers; 2.5M 8 layers; 8.3M 8 layers; 28M 8 layers; 21M 1 layer; 33M 2 and 4 layers

training.wall_clock: at most 30 hours per model (Section 4); under a day on a single GPU (intro)

other.scaling_study: for each FLOP budget pick the model/steps with lowest validation loss; layers 2,4,8,12; hidden 64..2048; plot shows polynomial dependence, no exponent reported

inference.decoding: zero temperature for most shown completions
inference.temperature: 0 for shown examples; 1 for GPT-Eval; 0.5 and 0.8 in single examples
inference.samples: 10 completions per prompt at temperature 1, GPT-4 scores averaged
inference.prompting: GPT-4 grader prompt: teacher/student framing with *** separator, asks verbal assessment then grades grammar, creativity, consistency (plus plot for Instruct) and age group A-F

other.truncation: GPT-Neo/GPT-2 outputs truncated at repeated 4-gram before grading (Fig 4 caption)

metrics.name: GPT-Eval grammar/creativity/consistency/plot
metrics.definition: GPT-4 grade out of 10 for each completion, averaged over 10 completions per prompt

metrics.name: Rouge-2 precision R_{2,p}
metrics.definition: fraction of 2-grams of T1 contained in T2

metrics.name: Rouge-2 F-measure
metrics.definition: harmonic mean of the two directional precisions

eval.protocol: GPT-4 grading with no human validation; diversity: 100 random training stories cut at ~40% and completed; single run per model, no seeds or CIs reported.

prompts.text: Write a short story (3-5 paragraphs) which only uses very simple words that a 3 year old child would likely understand. The story should use the verb "decorate", the noun "thunder" and the adjective "ancient". The story should have the following features: the story should contain at least one dialogue, the story has a bad ending. Remember to only use simple words!

Now, grade the student's completion in terms of grammar, creativity, consistency with the story's beginning and whether the plot makes sense. Moreover, please provide your best guess of what the age of the student might be, as reflected from the completion.

results.claim: Models below 10M parameters (embedding dim 256) or with one transformer block produce fluent, consistent stories.
results.setup: TinyStories-trained GPT-Neo models, qualitative plus GPT-4 grading
results.quote: below 10 million parameters with an embedding dimension of 256

results.claim: A 1-layer 21M model is competent enough to produce coherent stories; a 28M model is compared with GPT2-XL (1.5B) on one prompt.
results.setup: Single manually composed prompt, Figure 1, zero temperature
results.quote: a 28M parameter model trained on TinyStories3 with that of GPT2-XL, which is two orders of magnitude bigger

results.claim: Training takes at most 30 hours on one V100 for all Section 4 models.
results.quote: All of the models can be trained on a single V100 GPU within at most 30 hours.

results.claim: Consistency emerges when hidden size rises from 64 to 128; grammar saturates earlier than consistency and creativity.
results.setup: GPT-Eval scores in Fig 4 / 'Table 4' (image, numbers not in text)
results.quote: emerges when the hidden size of the model increases from 64 to 128
results.note: The paper calls the score grid both Table 4 and Figure 4.

results.claim: The largest model (about 80M) reaches almost perfect grammar and consistency but falls well short of GPT-4 on creativity.
results.quote: the largest model that we have trained on TinyStories (with roughly 80M parameters)

results.claim: 1-layer models struggle with instruction following; 2 layers give some ability.
results.quote: models that have only 1 layer seem to struggle quite substantially with following instructions

results.claim: Facts depend more on embedding dimension, context tracking more on number of layers.
results.setup: Hand-coloured success/failure of continuations for a small set of prompts (Figs 9-11)
results.quote: knowledge of facts seems to rely more on the embedding dimension, whereas for context-tracking the number of layers is more important

results.claim: Model trained without Summary+Words combinations still follows both instructions together.
results.quote: the model is able to follow these two types of instructions simultaneously even if it has never been trained on such a task

results.claim: Most 4- and 5-grams in generations never appear in the training data.
results.setup: 100 training stories cut at ~40% as prompts, Rouge/k-gram counts, Fig 16
results.quote: most of the 4, 5-grams in the models’ generations do not even appear once in the entire training data

results.claim: Closest training story to a generated completion has Rouge-2 precision 0.29 in the shown example.
Eval loss, grammar, creativity and consistency improve as attention heads increase from 2 to 8 (hidden 768).
results.setup: Fig 24 table: hidden 768, layers 1 and 2, heads 2/4/8; e.g. 2 layers eval loss 1.38 (2 heads) to 1.33 (8 heads)
results.quote: increasing it improves the performance of the model across all metrics

results.claim: A polynomial scaling law between best model size and FLOPs appears, from a small number of points.
results.setup: Layers 2,4,8,12; hidden 64..2048; best-loss model per FLOP budget
results.quote: the plot points to a polynomial dependence
results.note: Text refers to Figure 6 but the plot is Figure 23; no exponent is given.

limits: Cannot rule out complex template matching: 'we are not able to completely rule out the possibility that the models perform complex template matching'
Dataset size, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, steps and tokens are not stated
Evaluation relies on GPT-4 graders with no human validation, about 50 prompts, and single runs without variance
Many claims rest on a handful of hand-picked completions, coloured by hand
Scaling law has few points; interpretability section is explicitly preliminary
Authors say the paper does not show whether synthetic refined data helps practical uses

terms.definition: framework where GPT-4 grades a model's story completion like a teacher grading a student, on grammar, creativity, consistency, with an age-group guess
variant of TinyStories in which each story is preceded by instructions (words, sentence, features, summary)

lineage.quote: We use GPT-Neo architecture with window size 256 and context length 512.

lineage.work: Holtzman et al. neural text degeneration
Li et al. visualizing neural models in NLP
